query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored phase‐selective recrystallization of an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy can simultaneously boost both its strength and ductility by refining the soft phase while retaining the intact hard lamellar network.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a lamellar microstructure composed of alternating soft face-centered cubic (FCC) and hard B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment (potentially following cryo-rolling) designed to selectively recrystallize only the soft FCC phase without altering the hard phase, thereby creating a dual-scale (hierarchical) microstructure.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be performed under precisely optimized annealing temperatures and durations that permit recrystallization of the soft phase with minimal grain coarsening and no detrimental transformation of the hard phase, likely at intermediate temperatures below full recrystallization of the B2 phase.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically modified microstructure in which a fine-grained, recrystallized soft phase is embedded within a continuous network of preserved hard lamellae, promoting effective strain partitioning.
generation.mechanism: Selective recrystallization refines the soft phase, increasing its strain hardening capacity and ductility, while the contiguous hard phase acts as a reinforcing skeleton that sustains high strength through load transfer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a significant increase in yield strength (on the order of approximately 25% improvement) and greater uniform elongation (up to about 35%), thereby overcoming the conventional strength-ductility trade-off.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloys with coarse lamellar microstructures that display a limited combination of high strength and high ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only when the processing window is precisely maintained; over-annealing or full recrystallization (affecting both phases) may nullify the dual-phase synergy.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing parameters (temperature, duration) to achieve optimal phase selectivity and the quantitative magnitude of improvement require further empirical determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical as-cast eutectic HEA samples. Subject one set to the controlled phase-selective recrystallization protocol and the other set to a conventional full annealing treatment. Perform detailed microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to assess the grain sizes and phase distributions in the soft and hard phases, followed by mechanical testing (tensile tests) to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility.
measurements: Grain size and phase morphology of the FCC and B2 regions (via TEM/SEM)
Load–displacement curves and tensile properties (yield strength, UTS, uniform elongation)
Phase fraction analysis pre- and post-treatment (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples undergoing phase-selective recrystallization do not exhibit a significantly refined soft phase accompanied by a preserved hard phase (relative to the baseline) and fail to show a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility compared to fully annealed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. Phase-selective recrystallization makes eutectic high-entropy alloys ultra-ductile

Abstract: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa.
